title: Risk-adapted MRI Protocols for the Detection of Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Purpose To compare the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of three MRI protocols for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) according to prebiopsy risk. Materials and Methods This retrospective study included 390 male patients who underwent prostate multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) between January 2019 and April 2024 for suspected csPCa, followed by biopsy. Patients were stratified by Rotterdam Prostate Cancer Risk Calculator score into low-risk (<4%), intermediate-risk (4%-9%), and high-risk (≥10%) groups. Three datasets were generated from each examination: mpMRI (T2-weighted imaging, diffusion-weighted imaging [DWI], and dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging), unenhanced MRI (multiplanar T2-weighted imaging and DWI), and short MRI (axial T2-weighted imaging and DWI). Overall, 1170 datasets were randomly assigned to 10 expert radiologists (117 examinations each). Diagnostic performance for grade group 2 or greater cancer and clinical utility metrics were compared across risk groups. Results Among the 390 patients (median age, 66 years [IQR, 61-71 years]), csPCa prevalence was 34.4% (134 of 390). In low-risk patients, short MRI demonstrated the highest sensitivity (95% [21 of 22]), with no significant differences among protocols (all P ≥ .21) and greatest potential for safe biopsy avoidance (84 biopsies avoided per missed csPCa). In intermediate-risk patients, mpMRI showed higher sensitivity (83% vs 72% for unenhanced MRI and 62% for short MRI; P = .012 for mpMRI vs short MRI) and higher biopsy efficiency (1.11 vs 0.85 for mpMRI vs unenhanced MRI). In high-risk patients, protocol-related differences were minimal (all P ≥ .12). Conclusion mpMRI was associated with improved sensitivity and biopsy efficiency in intermediate-risk patients, whereas protocol differences were limited in low- and high-risk groups; these findings support risk-adapted selection of MRI protocols. Keywords: MR-Dynamic Contrast-enhanced, MR Imaging, Urinary, Prostate, Neoplasms-Primary, Efficacy Studies, Prostatic Neoplasms, MRI, Contrast Medium, Biopsy, Risk Assessment Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Causes of False-Negative Screening Digital Breast Tomosynthesis Examinations: A Multireader Study.
abstract: Purpose To classify the causes and pathologic characteristics of false-negative screening digital breast tomosynthesis examinations. Materials and Methods All false-negative screening examinations at a single center from March 1, 2019, through December 31, 2023, were collected. Seven fellowship-trained breast radiologists independently reviewed the false-negative screening and diagnostic mammograms preceding biopsy. For each mammogram, radiologists recorded the cancer as visible or not visible. Cancers were classified as mammographically occult (not visible on mammogram), missed (visible on screening mammogram), or true interval cancers (visible on diagnostic mammogram only). Between-classification comparisons were performed with the Pearson χ 2 test or analysis of variance. Results A total of 117 female patients (median age, 60 years [IQR, 49-70 years]) with false-negative screening mammograms were included. Most cancers manifested symptomatically (88 of 117, 75.2%) a median of 237 days (IQR, 187-301 days) after screening mammography. Among cancers, 47.9% (56 of 117), 26.5% (31 of 117), and 25.6% (30 of 117) were missed, mammographically occult, and true interval cancers, respectively. True interval cancers were more often estrogen receptor- (50.0% [15 of 30] vs 16.1% [five of 31] vs 21.8% [12 of 55]) and progesterone receptor-negative (66.7% [20 of 30] vs 22.6% [seven of 31] vs 35.7% [20 of 56]) than mammographically occult and missed cancers. Mammographically occult cancers were more often stage T0 (32.3% [10 of 31] vs 7.1% [four of 56] vs 10.0% [three of 30]) and detected at MRI (48.4% [15 of 31] vs 3.6% [two of 56] vs 10.0% [three of 30]) and developed in younger female patients (51 vs 62 vs 59 years of age, all P < .05) than missed and true interval cancers. Conclusion Half of false-negative screening mammograms were missed, one-quarter were true interval, and one-quarter were mammographically occult cancer, with differences in pathologic characteristics. Keywords: Mammography, Screening © RSNA, 2026 See also the commentary by Elahi and Slanetz in this issue.

title: Robotic Flexible Ureteroscopy: A Step-by-Step Guide to the ILY® Platform.
abstract: Introduction Robotic flexible ureteroscopy (rfURS) is emerging as an alternative to manual flexible ureteroscopy for the treatment of upper urinary tract stones. Contemporary guidelines and reviews describe its potential ergonomic and radiation-related advantages, as well as comparable surgical outcomes (1-5). Initial clinical and simulation studies with the ILY® platform have demonstrated feasibility, safety, and a short learning curve, although standardized implementation remains limited (6-10). This video presents a step-by-step workflow for the safe and efficient use of the ILY® platform. Materials and methods A 43-year-old woman with a previous right double-J stent placed for obstructive pyelonephritis underwent rfURS for a 13-mm renal pelvic stone (1,497 HU; volume 1,214 mm³). The video demonstrates operating-room setup, robot calibration and sterile draping, robot positioning and fixation, docking to the ureteral access sheath and ureteroscope assembly, console-controlled navigation, laser lithotripsy, systematic renal inspection, and standardized undocking. A flexible suction sheath was used throughout the procedure. Results Draping and docking times were 167 and 645 seconds, respectively. Robotic console time was 115 minutes, including 52 minutes of laser lithotripsy at 8 Hz and 1.2 J. Basket extraction was not required. Undocking was completed in 74 seconds, and total operative time was 130 minutes. No intraoperative complications or troubleshooting events occurred. Postoperative day-1 computed tomography confirmed stone-free status. The patient was discharged at 36 hours postoperatively without complications, as graded by the Clavien-Dindo classification (11). Surgeon satisfaction was rated 8 out of 10. Conclusion rfURS using the ILY® platform was feasible, safe, and effective. A standardized step-by-step workflow may facilitate adoption, improve procedural consistency, and enhance surgeon ergonomics (12). rfURS represents a meaningful step toward autonomous surgery (13).

title: Outcome of Children Treated with Rituximab for Steroid-Resistant Nephrotic Syndrome: Renal Histopathology as a Response Marker.
abstract: Background Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) in children remains a major therapeutic challenge. Although calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) are commonly used as first-line therapy, a substantial proportion of patients fail to achieve remission, and prolonged use may result in nephrotoxicity. Rituximab has emerged as a potential therapeutic option for refractory SRNS; however, treatment responses appear variable, and the influence of underlying renal histopathology remains incompletely understood. Objectives To evaluate the association between renal histopathological findings and clinical response to rituximab in children with calcineurin inhibitor-resistant steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS). Methods Study Design and Setting:This prospective observational study was conducted between 2011 and 2020 at a university-affiliated tertiary pediatric nephrology center. The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of rituximab in children with calcineurin inhibitor-resistant steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) and to examine the association between renal histopathological findings and treatment response. Twenty-four children aged 2-12 years were enrolled.Follow-up:Patients were followed prospectively after completion of rituximab therapy through regular clinical and laboratory assessments. The mean follow-up duration after the last rituximab infusion was 5.1 years (range: 6 months-8 years).Treatment Response Definitions:Complete remission was defined according to International Pediatric Nephrology Association (IPNA) recommendations as a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) ≤20 mg/mmol (≤0.2 mg/mg) or negative/trace proteinuria on dipstick testing on at least three consecutive occasions.Partial remission was defined as a UPCR >20 mg/mmol but <200 mg/mmol together with serum albumin ≥30 g/L.No response was defined as failure to achieve either complete or partial remission.Genetic Evaluation:Genetic testing was performed in all patients with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), classic minimal change disease (MCD), and MCD with IgM deposition. No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants associated with monogenic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome were identified in the tested patients. Genetic testing was not performed in patients with IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy, C1q nephropathy, or dense deposit disease. Results Twenty-four children with SRNS were included (13 males and 11 females; age range 2-12 years). Histopathological diagnoses included focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) in 9 patients (37.5%), minimal change disease (MCD) in 4 (16.7%), MCD with IgM deposition in 6 (25.0%), dense deposit disease in 2 (8.3%), membranous nephropathy in 1 (4.2%), IgA nephropathy in 1 (4.2%), and C1q nephropathy in 1 (4.2%). Overall, 10 patients (41.7%) achieved complete remission and 3 (12.5%) achieved partial remission, predominantly among patients with MCD and MCD with IgM deposition. Responses were uncommon among patients with FSGS. Eleven patients (45.8%), all of whom were non-responders, progressed to end-stage kidney disease. No major adverse effects of rituximab were observed; mild infusion reactions occurred in three patients and mild cellulitis in one patient. Conclusion In this cohort of children with refractory SRNS, favorable responses to rituximab were observed predominantly among patients with CNI- resistant MCD and MCD with IgM deposition, whereas responses among patients with FSGS were uncommon. These findings suggest that renal histopathology may help identify patients more likely to benefit from rituximab therapy; however, the small sample size, heterogeneous histopathological distribution, and observational study design preclude definitive conclusions. Larger prospective multicenter studies incorporating comprehensive genetic evaluation are required to determine whether histopathology can serve as a reliable predictor of rituximab responsiveness.

title: Proximal Scaphoid Pole Reconstruction Utilizing Ipsilateral Proximal Hamate Autograft.
abstract: Proximal pole scaphoid fractures complicated by nonunion and osteonecrosis present a challenging scenario with few good reconstructive options, especially when the proximal fragment is small or fragmented1-4. The use of an ipsilateral proximal hamate osteochondral autograft has emerged as a promising technique for reconstructing the proximal scaphoid pole, with the potential to restore carpal mechanics while avoiding the morbidity associated with free vascularized bone grafts or distant autograft sites. The procedure involves replacing the diseased proximal scaphoid with a structurally matched osteochondral graft from the ipsilateral proximal hamate. After excising the necrotic or fragmented scaphoid pole, a size-matched graft-harvested with its attached volar capitohamate ligament-is rotated 180° on its longitudinal axis to replicate normal scaphoid anatomy. The defect is measured in 3 planes using the scapholunate joint (proximal) and viable distal scaphoid surface as boundaries. On the hamate, an osteotomy is marked 8 to 10 mm distal to its proximal tip, parallel to the articular surface. The volar capitohamate ligament is preserved to guide graft orientation and maintain stability. These measurements align with recent anatomic and biomechanical studies that have confirmed 6 to 10-mm grafts accurately reproduce scaphoid morphology without compromising carpal kinematics. The graft is then inserted into the defect and secured with rigid internal fixation (headless compression screws or Kirschner wires). Residual gaps may be filled with cancellous bone graft. Scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL) reconstruction is typically performed by suturing the hamate's volar capitohamate ligament to the dorsal SLIL remnant on the lunate with a 2-0 nonabsorbable suture. In patients with a partially intact SLIL, such as after failed fixation, the hamate graft alone may provide adequate stability, making formal reconstruction unnecessary. If intraoperative findings reveal dorsal scapholunate instability or an attenuated SLIL, reconstruction is indicated. Healthy, tensionable ligament remnants are repaired directly or reinforced with suture anchors. When dorsal fibers are deficient but volar remnants remain, the attached volar capitohamate ligament is used for reinforcement. For small defects, a micro-interference screw may be employed for fixation. Postoperatively, the wrist is immobilized in a cast. When radiographic evidence of union is observed, the cast is removed and the patient begins a structured hand therapy program. Alternatives include vascularized and nonvascularized bone grafts (e.g., iliac crest), a vascularized medial femoral trochlear osteochondral flap, costochondral rib graft, proximal row carpectomy, and wrist arthrodesis1,2. These may be limited by donor-site morbidity, complexity, or suboptimal restoration of wrist biomechanics. The articular surface of the proximal hamate closely matches the curvature and size of the proximal pole of the scaphoid, making it an ideal structural substitute. The use of an articular autograft from the same wrist avoids the need for distant donor sites and microsurgical anastomoses, reducing overall morbidity. Additionally, because the graft is harvested with its volar ligament attached, it enables a simultaneous SLIL reconstruction, addressing carpal instability in a way that standard bone grafts cannot. This technique is relatively straightforward and reproducible, and it is especially beneficial in young, active patients with an irreparable proximal scaphoid, offering a chance to heal the nonunion and preserve near-normal wrist function without resorting to salvage procedures. Radiographic union is expected in the majority of cases within 8 to 12 weeks. Published series have demonstrated union rates of >90%, improved pain, restoration of near-normal wrist kinematics, and substantial improvements in range of motion and grip strength, although not always to the level of the contralateral wrist. Complications are rare but include nonunion, donor-site pain, and persistent stiffness. title: All-Suture Fixation for Acute Turf Toe Injuries.
abstract: Turf toe is a hallux metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ) injury caused by hyperextension of the great toe with axial loading1,2. High-grade injuries may threaten return to sport and require surgery3,4. Here, we describe a capsular reconstruction of the great toe MTPJ with all-knotless suture anchors and suture tape augmentation for turf toe injuries, in isolation or in combination with a traumatic bunion, designed to reduce suture burden, minimize soft-tissue irritation, and facilitate recovery. The procedure begins with the patient supine. A direct medial approach to the hallux MTPJ is performed. Both the medial base of the proximal phalanx and the medial eminence of the metatarsal head are drilled at isometric points, and augmentation with suture tape is then performed. Isometric drill holes are placed in the medial proximal phalanx base and metatarsal head for suture tape augmentation. A knotless suture anchor is placed approximately 3 mm proximal to the articular margin of the metatarsal head, repairing the medial capsule in a horizontal mattress fashion. An additional knotless anchor is placed at the plantar plate insertion, and the suture is passed through the tibial sesamoid sling and tensioned with the toe in 20° of plantar flexion. Suture tape is secured into the proximal phalanx with an interference screw, then passed through the deep capsule into the metatarsal head, followed by the placement of an additional interference screw into the metatarsal head. The anchor is inserted into the plantar-medial proximal phalanx at the flexor hallucis brevis insertion. The toe is flexed during tensioning, then adjusted per clinical examination and the sesamoid location beneath the metatarsal head. Knotless fixation permits incremental tensioning with intraoperative assessment of motion. Final tensioning is performed with the toe in neutral to correct deformity without overconstraint, preserving range of motion. Nonoperative alternatives include rest, ice, compression and elevation; anti-inflammatory drugs; activity modification; and brief immobilization5,6. Operative alternatives include primary capsuloligamentous complex repair with nonabsorbable sutures, plantar plate advancement with bone tunnels or suture anchors if primary repair is not feasible, and concomitant procedures such as sesamoidectomy and bunionectomy based on the injury pattern2,7,8. This technique is intended for high-grade turf toe injuries with capsuloligamentous disruption, sesamoid complex insufficiency, and MTPJ instability. Nonoperative treatment may be appropriate in cases of low-grade injury; however, persistent pain, instability, or loss of push-off strength following nonoperative treatment would indicate a higher-grade injury. Compared with isolated repair or plantar plate advancement alone, this technique restores both static and dynamic stabilizers of the hallux MTPJ while addressing associated angular deformity. Suture tape augmentation resists recurrent hyperextension and valgus forces while allowing controlled physiologic motion. Knotless, low-profile suture anchors minimize bulk and hardware prominence in a region with limited soft-tissue coverage and bone stock. This construct offers a robust reconstruction option for athletes requiring predictable restoration of stability and reliable return to sport. Operative treatment of high-grade turf toe injuries has been shown to result in reliable pain relief, restored stability, and high rates of return to sport8. Previous studies have suggested improved function and earlier return to play compared with prolonged nonoperative treatment in appropriate patients6,7. Knotless suture anchors reduce implant prominence and eliminate knot-related irritation, while the small insertional diameter of the suture anchors preserves bone stock in the metatarsal head and proximal phalanx. This construct provides immediate stability while allowing controlled motion, facilitating rehabilitation, and reducing postoperative stiffness. Athletes typically return to unrestricted activity within 6 to 9 months, aided by the suture tape augmentation allowing earlier movement through the range of motion. This augmentation reduces the need for long-term spica splinting and bracing and reduces the risk of recurrence. title: Morphometric Brain Networks at Ultra-Low Field: A First Assessment of Feasibility and Reliability
abstract: Background: Ultra-low field (ULF) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers accessible point-of-care neuroimaging, yet its capability to support multivariate network analyses remains understudied. Methods: We systematically evaluated the feasibility and reliability of Morphometric Similarity Networks (MSN) and Morphometric Inverse Divergence (MIND) networks derived from paired high-field (HF, 3T/1.5T) and ULF (64mT) scans in a primary cohort(N=23) and an independent replication cohort (N=19). We tested the impact of super-resolution processing, cortical parcellation granularity (Desikan-Killiany vs. Destrieux), and mesh resolution (fsnative vs. fsaverage5) on edge-level cross-scanner agreement (Lin's concordance correlation coefficient, CCC) and subject-level identifiability. Results: MIND networks demonstrated higher edge-level HF-ULF agreement (mean CCC = 0.95) and ULF reproducibility (mean CCC = 0.98) compared to MSNs (mean CCC = 0.86-0.87 and 0.91-0.94, respectively). In contrast, MSNs yielded higher subject-level differential identifiability across field strengths due to a broader distinction between within- and between-subject similarity. Reconstructing MIND networks on native high-resolution meshes (fsnative) maximised cross-scanner agreement, whereas coarser meshes and finer cortical parcellations enhanced individual network identifiability. Conclusions: Structural similarity networks can be reliably constructed from ULF MRI data. Optimal analytic choices depend on study objectives: MIND on native meshes maximises cross-scanner stability, whereas MSNs excel at preserving individual uniqueness, paving the way for globally scalable connectomic research.

title: ACorD: Adaptive Correspondence Discovery for Medical Image Registration
abstract: Medical image registration is a fundamental task for aligning anatomical structures across images. Exhaustively searching for point-wise correspondences is prohibitively expensive in both computation and memory, particularly for high-resolution 3D medical images. Most recent learning-based methods directly predict correspondences in a coarse-to-fine manner, but often propagate intermediate estimates across scales without explicitly weighting correspondence evidence, which can allow coarse-scale errors to persist during refinement. To address these challenges, we propose ACorD, an adaptive correspondence discovery framework designed to mitigate error propagation with an attention-guided process. ACorD first predicts multiple potential correspondence candidates through Correlation-guided Cross-scale Offset Prediction (CCOP), which combines correlation maps as spatial matching priors with cross-scale features as global deformation context. Then, Multi-Head Deformable Aggregation (MHDA) aggregates these candidate correspondences using attention, producing a learned, non-uniform weighting over competing matches rather than treating them equally. The multi-head design further captures complementary deformation patterns, ensuring both global alignment and local precision. By integrating adaptive offset prediction with selective, attention-based aggregation of correspondence evidence, ACorD enables accurate deformation refinement. Extensive experiments on four public medical registration benchmarks demonstrate that adaptive correspondence discovery within a multi-scale refinement framework improves registration robustness across diverse anatomical structures.

title: Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient MCI Conversion Prediction
abstract: Allocating limited trainable capacity across convolutional layers is a central challenge in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of pretrained three-dimensional (3D) networks. We propose Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation, which jointly selects input- and output-channel ranks under a fixed adapter-parameter budget while preserving the spatial kernel modes. To guide rank selection, we learn task-specific proxy updates from downstream training data and approximate them using candidate Tucker rank pairs. A perturbation analysis bounds the output discrepancy between the fixed proxy network and its Tucker approximation in terms of layerwise reconstruction residuals, motivating residual-based allocation. We normalize each squared residual by the corresponding proxy-update energy to compare relative approximation errors across layers. Dynamic programming minimizes their sum under a global budget constraint that accounts for both channel factors and the Tucker core. This yields a globally optimal allocation over the specified candidate rank pairs. We evaluate the method on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort for predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease within 36 months, using hippocampal segmentation pretraining. Across five random seeds, the proposed method achieves a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.7706, compared with 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning. The total number of trainable parameters is limited to approximately 0.618 million, accounting for only 1.45% of the full model. Adaptive Tucker rank allocation thus provides an effective approach to parameter-efficient transfer learning in 3D medical imaging.

title: How Robust Are Prognostic Radiomic Features? Comparing Selection Techniques on Pooled Glioblastoma Cohorts
abstract: Radiomic survival studies in glioblastoma report heterogeneous prognostic features, but how much of this stems from the methodology itself is rarely examined. We analysed the association of 463 radiomic, anatomical and clinical features from pre-treatment MRI with overall survival in 705 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients from three public cohorts, using three techniques: a log-rank test after median split, univariate Cox regression (both Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) and an XGBoost regressor interpreted with SHAP. The log-rank test selected 99 features, Cox regression 72 and SHAP its top 20; five were selected by all three: age, a peritumoural T2 texture feature, the number of connected peritumoural mask components and two image-level intensity maxima. The two survival tests shared 51 features, about half of the SHAP top 20 were also selected by either test, and where selections overlapped, effect directions agreed. Many selections were PyRadiomics diagnostic descriptors that are not restricted to tumour voxels. Analytical pipeline choices, including ranking method, pre-filtering and descriptor handling, can substantially influence which features appear prognostic.

title: XGLASS: X-Ray, Gaze and Language Assisted Slice Sequencing for CT Volumes
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve remarkable performance on 2D medical images, such as X-rays or pathology images, while 3D VLMs that directly process CT/MRI volumes lag behind due to limited 3D training data and the predominance of 2D foundation architectures. To leverage powerful 2D VLMs for analyzing medical volumes, which contain hundreds of slices, it is therefore necessary to focus only on those few slices, which are diagnostically relevant. To enable such a prioritization, we propose XGLASS, a method that transfers medical expertise from 2D X-rays to 3D CT for task-aware slice prioritization. XGLASS uses disease-conditioned importance maps derived from language-aligned radiologist gaze on X-rays and spatially aligns them with coronal CT projections, bringing gaze priors and CT content into a shared 2D representation. The fused gaze-prior/CT projection is then used to predict a disease-specific ordering of axial slices, prioritizing diagnostically relevant slices. XGLASS significantly improves budgeted retrieval over 2D and 3D-native baselines, achieving a top-10 hit rate up to 75.9% for the best-performing disease. In practice, this means that after inspecting only the top 10 slices (4.17% of a 240-slice scan), XGLASS identifies a diagnostically relevant slice in more than 75% of cases. For downstream slice-wise finding classification, an XGLASS-selected 30-slice candidate set reduces model calls by 87.5% while improving F1 by 11.3 percentage points over all-slice inference, 4.2 points over the strongest 2D selector, and remains competitive with 3D-native selectors while requiring up to 130.8 times less time and 10.9 times less GPU memory per finding, supporting its use as a lightweight preselector for volumetric CT analysis. The code and pretrained checkpoint are available on https://github.com/michaelgloeckler/XGLASS.

title: TIM: Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model for Longitudinal Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) aims to translate medical images into diagnostic text, reducing radiologists' workload and standardizing clinical documentation. Nonetheless, existing approaches mainly focus on single-timepoint analysis and fail to capture temporal disease evolution across longitudinal examinations. While recent longitudinal RRG (LRRG) approaches incorporate historical data, they often combine images from different time points within a single representation space, leading to blurred semantics and inconsistent temporal reasoning. In this work, we propose a Temporal Decoupling with Iterative Mutual-Refinement Model (TIM), a two-stage framework that explicitly decouples spatial pathology from temporal progression and iteratively refines reports through mutual feedback. Stage I performs temporal-decoupled representation learning, separating temporal evolution patterns from disease-specific features and generating radiology reports for both prior and current studies. Stage II introduces a mutual report refinement mechanism that identifies diagnostic inconsistencies within prior reports and iteratively rectifies both prior and current reports through error-sensitive feedback. Experiments on the Longitudinal-MIMIC dataset demonstrate that TIM surpasses existing single-image and longitudinal baselines, achieving new state-of-the-art performance across both language and clinical metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/yihengd/TIM.

title: MCDA: Multi-View Graph Contrastive Learning with Dynamic Topology Augmentation for Functional MRI Analysis
abstract: Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) is a vital non-invasive tool for diagnosing brain disorders and uncovering pathological mechanisms. However, existing graph contrastive learning (GCL) methods often underexploit augmentation histories across training epochs and the relationships among different augmented views. In this paper, we introduce a topology-guided Multi-view graph Contrastive learning framework with Dynamic graph topology Augmentation (MCDA) for fMRI analysis. Unlike traditional GCL that uses fixed noise or edge-dropping, MCDA employs a Dynamic Augmentation Update (DAU) module that iteratively refines the augmented topology. Specifically, we incorporate self-aware and cross-sample augmentation strategies to simultaneously capture individual-specific functional signatures and inter-subject heterogeneity. We then design a topology-guided multi-view graph contrastive learning scheme that explores interrelationships not only between the original network and its augmented views, but also across different augmented views to maximize structural information preservation. We characterize the score-level optimization directions and establish a lower bound for the contrastive objective. The framework combines classification and contrastive losses for brain disorder diagnosis and examines discriminative functional connectivity patterns as potential biomarkers. Experiments on two public rs-fMRI datasets comprising 1,236 subjects demonstrate that MCDA outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. The code has been made publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/goodcodingagoodboy/MCDA}.

title: HGASurv: Hierarchical Granularity-Aware Integration for Multimodal Survival Prediction
abstract: Objective: Multimodal survival prediction jointly analyzes histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), genomic profiles, and clinical variables to stratify patients by risk. However, existing approaches often inadequately account for granularity differences across modalities, particularly in spatial organization and feature dimensionality. To address these challenges, we propose HGASurv, which introduces a hierarchical WSI encoding module and a clinical-guided graph propagation module for granularity-aware multimodal integration. Methods: The hierarchical WSI encoding module maps WSI patch features onto a spatial grid using their original coordinates and applies parallel convolutions to construct representations at patch, local-neighborhood, and regional scales. Genomic signature embeddings then query these scale-specific WSI representations through cross-modal co-attention, producing signature-conditioned morphological features. The clinical-guided graph propagation module uses clinical variables to define patient-similarity edges and propagates fused image-genomic node embeddings with graph attention, integrating clinical information through topology rather than feature concatenation. Results: Across three TCGA cohorts, HGASurv achieved the strongest overall C-index performance, with ablation studies supporting the complementary contributions of the hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation modules. Conclusion and Significance: By introducing hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation, HGASurv unifies multi-scale pathology representation with topology-based clinical integration in a hierarchical granularity-aware framework. This design shows that matching representation and integration mechanisms to modality-specific granularity improves multimodal survival prediction.

title: Progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory for incomplete multimodal brain tumor segmentation
abstract: Brain tumor segmentation uses complementary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequences, but some sequences may be unavailable in practice. Their absence changes the information available for segmenting different tumor regions. Fusion methods can support different input subsets. However, fusion at several scales does not by itself specify how tumor evidence is retained and updated to guide fusion at later stages. We propose a progressive multi-scale tumor-state memory network (PMTM) for segmentation from any non-empty subset of T1ce, T1, FLAIR, and T2. PMTM maintains a compact state for the current subject across the encoder stages. At each stage, we use assignment maps to pool spatial features into ordered evidence vectors for each available modality. We average these vectors across the available modalities, and a learned gate combines this evidence with the previous state. The up- dated state guides residual fusion at that stage and is used in the state update at the next stage. A modality-token mixer also models interactions among the available modalities at each stage. We apply semantic supervision to the assignment maps at all four stages. We evaluate PMTM on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI across all 15 non-empty modality subsets. Averaged over the three tumor regions and the 15 subsets, PMTM achieves Dice scores of 75.31%, 77.54%, and 80.47% on BraTS2018, BraTS2020, and BraTS2023 GLI, respectively. These scores are higher than those of RobustSeg, RFNet, and mmFormer in our experiments on each dataset. Component ablations and internal state analysis are performed on BraTS2020.

title: 3D Diffusion Models for Medical Imaging
abstract: Generative deep learning methods such as Variational Autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks or Diffusion Models have achieved remarkable results in image synthesis. In particular, Diffusion Models have demonstrated superior image fidelity and sample diversity compared to other approaches on standard benchmarks, while also offering more flexible training dynamics as evidenced both in natural image domains and in medical applications. In medical imaging including Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Positron Emission Tomography, such models have various important use-cases including data augmentation, domain transfer, image reconstruction, inpainting, image augmentation and artifact correction. Further, generated images can be conditioned on patient characteristics, medical reports, segmentation masks or other images. Specific challenges arise due to the 3D volumetric nature of medical images, which translate to substantial demands in terms of memory, compute, and training data. This article provides a comparative overview of 3D Diffusion Models which have been developed for medical images, with a focus on current performance, limitations, and an outlook for future work.

In medical imaging including Computed Tomography, Magnetic Resonance Imaging or Positron Emission Tomography, such models have various important use-cases including data augmentation, domain transfer, image reconstruction, inpainting, image augmentation and artifact correction. Further, generated images can be conditioned on patient characteristics, medical reports, segmentation masks or other images. Specific challenges arise due to the 3D volumetric nature of medical images, which translate to substantial demands in terms of memory, compute, and training data. This article provides a comparative overview of 3D Diffusion Models which have been developed for medical images, with a focus on current performance, limitations, and an outlook for future work.

title: MRI Reconstruction Risk Estimation from Inference Dynamics
abstract: Iterative MRI reconstructors produce intermediate estimates before returning a final image. We study these inference trajectories as a model-internal representation of realized reconstruction risk, measured by log-NMSE. Model-native states are projected to magnitude images, summarized by a fixed 16-dimensional descriptor, and mapped to risk using a source-trained ridge readout. Across three reconstruction backbones, trajectory features are strongly predictive of reconstruction risk on held-out source data. Under zero-shot target shift, their behavior is backbone-dependent, exhibiting both preserved positive association and readout reversal. Conditional analyses show that trajectory information can remain associated with error beyond an initialization-only predictor. A prefix analysis further shows that useful trajectory information can emerge before reconstruction completes. Repeated-mask and low-shot calibration studies indicate that trajectories primarily encode persistent case difficulty, while their orientation and calibration can change under domain shift.

title: Scaling Vision Foundation Models for Toxicologic Pathology
abstract: Here, we present TOX-FM, a family of non-clinical PFMs trained on large-scale diverse histopathology datasets of over one million whole slide images consisting of over 60 organs across six animal species from over 14,000 toxicology studies across six decades. We introduce a comprehensive benchmark of 18 non-clinical downstream tasks, incorporate an established benchmark of 9 clinical downstream tasks, and evaluate TOX-FM against state-of-the-art clinical PFMs across both non-clinical and clinical domains. Notably, we explore open questions surrounding domain-specific training and cross-domain generalization, offering insights into the opportunities and challenges of applying PFMs in the non-clinical domain.

title: Seven Novel Sonographic Signs
abstract: Ultrasound is a widely used imaging modality in clinical practice, and sonographic signs serve as valuable teaching tools that aid in pattern recognition and diagnosis. This review consolidates five novel sonographic signs previously proposed by the author, including the Cracked Earth Sign for subcutaneous edema, the Mushroom Cap Sign for localized gallbladder adenomyomatosis, the LTS Sign for dilated cardiomyopathy, the LTI Sign for endocardial fibroelastosis, and the Three Pipes Sign for the suprasternal long-axis view of the aortic arch. The SFH Sign for advanced cervical insufficiency and the Gentle Wave Sign for the tardus-parvus waveform are proposed for the first time in this paper. Collectively, these seven signs span the fields of superficial ultrasound, abdominal ultrasound, echocardiography, and obstetric ultrasound. For each sign, its naming logic, definition, clinical implications, and teaching value are described. This review aims to facilitate a better understanding of these signs and to promote their use as teaching aids in ultrasound education.

title: Enhancing Structural Quality in Medical X-ray Super-Resolution via Domain-Aware Loss
abstract: Abstract Upscaling medical X-ray images is more challenging than enhancing natural images, because preserving accurate structural and boundary information is more important for diagnostic correctness than producing a realistic appearance. Super-resolution methods such as SRGAN, ESRGAN, and the Hybrid Attention Transformer (HAT) perform well on natural images, but when applied to medical images they can cause texture hallucination, obscure anatomical boundaries, and remove clinically important features. This study presents a comprehensive comparison of four approaches: standard SRGAN, standard ESRGAN with VGG-based perceptual loss, HAT with L1 loss, and the proposed optimised models ESRGAN_USELoss and HAT_USELoss, which incorporate a domain-specific loss function designed for X-ray imaging. The proposed USELoss (U-Net, Sobel and Edge Loss) replaces the computationally heavy VGG19 perceptual loss with a lightweight U-Net encoder that preserves multi-scale anatomical structures, and adds a Sobel-based edge loss to improve boundary accuracy, prioritising diagnostic fidelity over perceptual sharpness. On the PadChest X-ray dataset the quantitative results show large gains: standard ESRGAN reaches only 22.21 dB PSNR, whereas ESRGAN_USELoss reaches 34.04 dB, while HAT_USELoss achieves the best SSIM (0.9215) and LPIPS (0.1607). The proposed methods improve edge-preservation metrics by 5.5%, demonstrating that domain-specific loss functions are effective for clinically reliable medical image super-resolution. https://github.com/1aryantyagi/Segmentation-Paper is the Github repository of the code.

title: Oral Foregut Duplicate cyst presenting as tongue-tie in a pediatric patient: a clinicopathologic case report
abstract: Abstract Oral foregut duplication cysts (OFDCs) are rare congenital anomalies arising from abnormal foregut development during embryogenesis, characterized by ectopic gastrointestinal or respiratory epithelium within the oral cavity. We present the case of a 6-year-old boy referred to with a presumptive diagnosis of ankyloglossia ("tongue-tie") who was found to have a well-circumscribed midline cystic mass within the intrinsic muscles of the tongue. MRI demonstrated a homogeneous T2-hyperintense, T1-isointense lesion with increased diffusivity and minimal wall enhancement. The mass was excised via a ventral tongue approach and delivered intact. Histopathologic examination revealed a cyst wall lined by ciliated respiratory-type epithelium with an underlying smooth muscular layer, consistent with an oral foregut duplication cyst. The differential diagnosis, including ranula, leiomyoma, rhabdomyoma, and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor, is discussed. This case highlights the importance of considering foregut duplication cysts in the differential diagnosis of congenital tongue masses, particularly when clinical presentation mimics ankyloglossia. Complete surgical excision is curative, with a low risk of recurrence.

title: Reproducibility-Aware Evaluation of Hierarchical Multiple- Instance Learning for Patient-Level Thrombosis Detection from Compression Ultrasound
abstract: Abstract Background To provide a reproducibility-aware evaluation of multi-site cine multiple-instance learning (MS-CineMIL) versus a fixed 8-frame imaging baseline under patient-level five-fold cross-validation, and to examine whether the nominal ROC AUC difference reproduces after field completion and runtime environment control. The study delineates aggregation applicability boundaries rather than presupposing a stable advantage. Methods The public ThrombUS+ Dataset #1 Training Set (v1.0; 594 subjects, 2,341 DICOM cine clips) was used. Thrombosis is a per-site label, so the patient-level endpoint was defined as engineering-positive: raw Thrombosis = 1 for any record of the same SubjectID (81/594). After quality control, 2,327 cines were retained. Partitions used SubjectID isolation. Primary metric: ROC AUC; secondary: PR AUC, Brier score. Model differences were tested by 10,000-resample patient-level paired bootstrap (empirical two-sided P values; Bonferroni α = 0.0167). Results In the V1 historical frozen analysis, the ROC AUC difference of MS-CineMIL versus the fixed 8-frame baseline was + 0.0740 (95% CI 0.0043 to 0.1454, P = 0.039), failing Bonferroni correction. In the same-environment controlled comparison, the difference was − 0.0283 (95% CI − 0.1177 to 0.0608, P = 0.538) with a larger Brier error (+ 0.0374, P < 0.001). The baseline re-run yielded 0.6390; the complete model ROC AUC was 0.6419. The between-run baseline shift (0.0711) matched the nominal gain (+ 0.0740); no stable advantage emerged. Conclusions The V1 frozen difference did not pass multiple-comparison correction, was not reproduced under controlled comparison, and was accompanied by a larger Brier error. Evidence supports boundary auditing of model components, field completeness, and aggregation strategies, but not stable superiority, clinical deployment, external applicability, or novelty claims.

title: Adenosquamous carcinoma of the colon with an aberrant MLH1 immunostaining pattern: a diagnostic pitfall in mismatch repair assessment
abstract: Abstract Background Adenosquamous carcinoma (ASC) is a rare histological subtype of colorectal cancer (CRC) that carries a poor prognosis and has been associated with a distinct molecular profile - higher frequency of mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR), PD-L1 overexpression, and KRAS mutations. With recent advances in CRC therapeutics, molecular characterization of rare histological subtypes has become increasingly important. Here, we report a case of colorectal ASC with a distinctive dMMR immunohistochemical profile and provide a review of the literature on this rare colorectal neoplasm. Case Presentation: We report the case of a 64-year-old woman who presented with a three-month history of worsening abdominal pain and recent-onset hematochezia. Abdominal CT revealed a large mass involving the right colon. She underwent a total pelvic exenteration. Histopathology showed a high-grade, poorly differentiated tumor with mixed glandular and squamous components, staged as pT4b pN1a. Immunohistochemistry confirmed both glandular and squamous differentiation. Mismatch repair protein analysis showed loss of PMS2 expression and a granular, dot-like MLH1 staining pattern—interpreted as loss of expression and consistent with a known clone-specific artifact—while MSH2 and MSH6 were retained, supporting a dMMR phenotype. The patient received mFLOX chemotherapy but died four months postoperatively due to disease-related complications. Discussion This case illustrates the classic clinicopathological features of ASC, alongside a dMMR immunoprofile that may carry therapeutic relevance given the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors in MSI-high colorectal tumors. The findings also underscore the importance of correctly recognizing clone-specific MLH1 staining artifacts, as misinterpretation could falsely suggest isolated PMS2 loss and trigger unnecessary germline testing for Lynch syndrome. Given the rarity of ASC and its limited molecular characterization, accurate MMR status assessment remains critical for guiding treatment decisions and avoiding diagnostic pitfalls.

title: Contour-free multi-instance learning versus conventional CT features for preoperative Ki-67 stratification in gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumors: a retrospective comparison
abstract: Abstract Background : Manual tumor contouring adds a separate preprocessing step to CT-based prediction. We therefore evaluated whether complete-series multiinstance learning (MIL) could perform preoperative Ki-67 stratification from dual-phase CT without tumor contours and provide greater discrimination than conventional CT features. Methods : This retrospective study included 61 patients. Ki-67 cutoffs of 5%, 8%, and 10% defined three cutoff-specific tasks. Patients whose reported Ki-67 interval spanned a cutoff were excluded only from the corresponding task. Twenty-one conventional variables were analyzed with two conventional models, and frozen ResNet-18 features from the complete arterial and venous phase series were analyzed separately with five MIL methods. Four prespecified equal-logit fusion combinations were evaluated. Patient-level stratified fivefold cross-validation was repeated 10 times. Assessment comprised AUROC, AUPRC, calibration assessment, decision-curve analysis, paired bootstrap comparisons with Holm correction, and a post-training attention audit. Results : The three tasks included 59, 54, and 56 patients, with 41, 26, and 15 positive cases. The highest AUROCs were 0.645 (95% CI, 0.485–0.781) at 5%, 0.646 (95% CI, 0.496–0.788) at 8%, and 0.605 (95% CI, 0.442–0.753) at 10%. The maximum AUPRCs at 5%, 8%, and 10% were 0.822, 0.637, and 0.346. Every AUROC confidence interval included 0.5, and no comparison among the prespecified individual models or between fusion and its components remained significant after Holm correction. In the attention audit, 34 of 60 tests remained significant after global Holm correction, with 21 estimates above and 13 below their prespecified references. Conclusions : Complete-series MIL was applied separately to arterial and venous CT series for cutoff-specific Ki-67 stratification and did not require tumor contour inputs. It showed no clear discrimination advantage over conventional CT features in this cohort. External validation and direct assessment of annotation burden are required before clinical use.

title: Correlation between Serum MMP-1/TIMP-1 Ratio and the Severity of Diabetic Retinopathy in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Abstract Background Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) is the leading cause of blindness among the working-age population. Current screening and grading primarily rely on fundus imaging, lacking serological markers that reflect early molecular pathological changes. There is an urgent need to identify biomarkers for early warning and progression assessment of DR. Purpose To investigate the correlation between serum levels of MMP-1, MMP-2, TIMP-1, and their ratios with the severity of DR in Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), providing serological references for early identification and risk assessment of DR progression. Methods and Results Sixty-four T2DM patients were enrolled and divided into three groups based on fundus findings: Non DR group (n = 31), non-proliferative DR (NPDR) group (n = 17), and proliferative DR (PDR) group (n = 16). Serum levels of MMP-1, MMP-2, and TIMP-1 were measured using ELISA, and the MMP-1/TIMP-1 and MMP-2/TIMP-1 ratios were calculated. Results showed that serum MMP-1 levels and the MMP-1/TIMP-1 ratio exhibited an increasing trend across the three groups and were significantly positively correlated with DR severity grading (r = 0.283, P = 0.023; r = 0.344, P = 0.005). No statistically significant differences were observed in MMP-2, TIMP-1 levels, or the MMP-2/TIMP-1 ratio among the groups, nor were they significantly correlated with DR severity. Conclusion Serum MMP-1 levels and the MMP-1/TIMP-1 ratio increase with the severity of DR and may serve as novel serological candidate markers for reflecting DR progression. The MMP-1/TIMP-1 ratio showed a stronger correlation than the single marker, suggesting its potential value as a comprehensive indicator of extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation and remodeling balance in assessing DR progression. Future studies with larger sample sizes and combined ocular local samples are needed for further validation.

title: Interpretable Concept-Bottleneck Vision-Language Model Predicts Pathologic Complete Response From Longitudinal Breast DCE-MRI
abstract: Abstract Deep learning can predict neoadjuvant treatment response in breast cancer, but most models are black boxes whose reasoning clinicians cannot verify, limiting adoption. We developed an interpretable concept-bottleneck vision-language model (CB-VLM) that predicts pathologic complete response (pCR) from pre-treatment and early-treatment dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI, routing every prediction through eleven radiologist-recognizable, BI-RADS-style imaging concepts plus age and molecular subtype. Trained on 753 patients from the multicenter I-SPY2 trial, the model achieved an AUROC of 0.76 on encoder-held-out data (n = 144) and generalized to an independent I-SPY1 cohort (AUC 0.71; n = 110). Accuracy rose with model confidence (88% versus 58% on borderline predictions), and early change in functional tumor volume was the dominant predictor across both cohorts. To our knowledge, this is the first large vision-language model to generate concept-grounded reasoning for breast DCE-MRI treatment response prediction, reframing a black-box task as transparent, auditable, and generalizable.

title: Thenar Muscle Thickness Assessed by Point-of-Care Ultrasound and Geriatric Vulnerability in Hospitalized Older Adults: A Pilot Study
abstract: Abstract Background Malnutrition and sarcopenia frequently coexist in hospitalized older adults. Thenar muscle thickness (TMT) may provide a pragmatic correlate of geriatric vulnerability, but its clinical relevance is unestablished. Methods This retrospective, single-centre, cross-sectional pilot study analyzed 50 hospitalized patients aged 75 years or older, admitted between October and December 2024. Unadjusted Spearman correlations assessed associations between TMT and Mini Nutritional Assessment–Short Form (MNA-SF), Braden, and Conley scores. Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals were calculated for these three correlations. Results Mean age was 86.2 years; 60.0% of participants were women. Mean TMT was 2.62 cm (SD, 0.48). Overall, 84.0% of patients were malnourished or at risk of malnutrition, 66.0% had high pressure-injury risk, and 90.0% had a Conley score indicating fall risk. Higher TMT correlated with higher MNA-SF (rho = 0.760; 95% CI, 0.595–0.859; P < 0.001) and Braden scores (rho = 0.560; 95% CI, 0.340–0.729; P < 0.001), and with lower Conley scores (Rho = − 0.406; 95% CI, − 0.627 to − 0.141; P = 0.003). Associations remained directionally consistent after adjustment for age and sex: partial rho was 0.753 (95% CI, 0.572–0.865) for MNA-SF, 0.510 (95% CI, 0.251–0.709) for Braden, and − 0.361 (95% CI, − 0.602 to − 0.054) for Conley. TMT was not significantly associated with length of stay (Rho = − 0.240; P = 0.093). Conclusions In very old hospitalized adults, lower TMT was associated with poorer nutritional status and greater fall and pressure-injury risk. TMT may complement multidimensional geriatric assessment, but the small, unadjusted pilot design and absence of a sarcopenia reference standard preclude diagnostic or independent prognostic claims.

TMT may complement multidimensional geriatric assessment, but the small, unadjusted pilot design and absence of a sarcopenia reference standard preclude diagnostic or independent prognostic claims.

title: Evaluating the Osteogenic potential of S. officinale against Glucocorticoid-induced Osteoporosis using in vivo model
abstract: Abstract Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis is characterized by impaired bone formation, increased bone resorption and disruption of bone mineralization. The present study investigated the osteoprotective potential of Symphytum officinale ( S. officinale ) aqueous root extract using a dexamethasone-induced osteoporosis model in adult zebrafish ( Danio rerio ). Phytochemical screening and LC–MS analysis were performed to characterize the extract, followed by developmental toxicity assessment. Adult zebrafish were divided into control, dexamethasone-treated and low- and high-dose S. officinale -treated groups. Bone regeneration and mineralization were evaluated using histopathology, Alizarin Red staining, scale morphometry and ICP-MS analysis of calcium and phosphorus. Hydroxyproline, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) assays were performed to assess collagen content and bone remodelling. The extract showed the presence of alkaloids, terpenoids, phytosterols and other bioactive constituents, including quercetin derivatives and biochanin A, while no developmental toxicity was observed at the tested concentrations. Dexamethasone induced marked alterations in tissue architecture, reduced mineral deposition and scale size and disrupted calcium and phosphorus levels. S. officinale treatment improved skeletal morphology, mineralization, scale size and mineral content, with pronounced effects on several parameters at the higher dose. The extract also modulated hydroxyproline, ALP and TRAP activities, indicating concentration-dependent effects on bone remodelling. Hence, S. officinale demonstrates osteoprotective potential against dexamethasone-induced skeletal alterations in zebrafish.

title: When tiny lungs Struggle to breathe; a rare cause of Refractory Primary Pulmonary Hypertension
abstract: Abstract Alveolar capillary dysplasia with malpositioned pulmonary veins (ACD/MPV) is a lethal congenital lung disorder with a mortality rate of almost 100%. Infants deteriorate within the first 24 hours of life. Here, we present a 2-day old female child born of full term normal vaginal delivery and cried immediately after birth. The baby presented with Respiratory distress within 6 hours of life and was put on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. 2-D echo revealed no congenital heart disease. The child continued to have pulmonary hypertension non-responsive to pharmacotherapy and eventually passed away. A post mortem histopathology examination revealed immature lung parenchyma with arrest in the saccular phase, thickened alveolar septae with abnormally positioned pulmonary capillaries. Focally, there were thin-walled vessels invested in the same adventitial sheath as the pulmonary arteries. The pulmonary arterioles exhibited features of pulmonary artery hypertension. Based on this constellation of features, the baby was diagnosed with ACD/MPV. The rarity and the focal nature of this condition make it a diagnostic challenge in terms of awareness of this entity and subsequent interpretation. Conclusion : This case reiterates the importance of knowing and understanding normal histology. A high degree of clinical suspicion as well as expertise in the field of thoracic pathology is required for appropriate diagnosis.

title: Possible Neurosarcoidosis Presenting with Chronic Pachymeningeal Disease, Extensive Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis, and Recurrent Seizures: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background: Neurosarcoidosis is an uncommon manifestation of sarcoidosis that can involve the meninges, cranial nerves, brain parenchyma, spinal cord, and cerebral vasculature. Its clinical and radiological manifestations frequently overlap with infectious, inflammatory, neoplastic, and vascular disorders, creating substantial diagnostic challenges. Case presentation: A 42-year-old woman presented with recurrent abnormal involuntary movements and progressive neurological deterioration. Her illness had evolved over approximately 12 years, beginning with chronic headache followed by right periorbital discomfort, progressive visual impairment, facial sensory symptoms, and later progressive focal neurological deficits. She was initially evaluated for a brain tumor and subsequently received prolonged anti-tuberculous therapy on more than one occasion for presumed tuberculous meningitis, with incomplete or absent clinical response. Over the months preceding the current admission, she developed progressive hemiparesis, abnormal posturing, facial twitching, dysarthria, urinary symptoms, and recurrent focal seizures that subsequently became prolonged and generalized with impaired consciousness. Serial brain imaging reported chronic pachymeningeal and leptomeningeal enhancement, cortical and subcortical abnormalities, features of raised intracranial pressure, and progressive vascular complications. Contrast-enhanced CT subsequently demonstrated superior sagittal sinus and bilateral cavernous sinus thrombosis with multifocal cerebral venous infarction/edema and small bilateral hemispheric and tentorial/interhemispheric subdural hematomas. Laboratory evaluation did not demonstrate a clear alternative infectious or systemic autoimmune etiology. A skin punch biopsy of healed chest lesions showed a sclerosing/keloidal scar without histological evidence of sarcoidosis or tuberculosis. Abdominopelvic ultrasonography additionally demonstrated chronic portal vein occlusion/thrombosis with periportal collateral vessels and periportal fibrosis. In the context of the prolonged clinical course, longitudinal meningeal imaging abnormalities, exclusion of several important mimickers, and multidisciplinary reassessment, a working diagnosis of possible neurosarcoidosis was made. Anti-tuberculous therapy was discontinued. The patient was treated with high-dose corticosteroids followed by oral prednisone and early steroid-sparing methotrexate with folic acid. At four-month follow-up, she demonstrated substantial clinical improvement, including recovery of baseline mentation, resolution of severe headache, cessation of clinical seizures, improvement in motor weakness and abnormal movements, and improvement/stabilization of visual and functional symptoms. Conclusion: This case illustrates the diagnostic complexity of chronic meningeal inflammatory disease presenting with progressive neurological dysfunction and extensive cerebral venous thrombosis. Persistent pachymeningeal abnormalities, failure to respond to prolonged anti-tuberculous treatment, and progressive neurological manifestations should prompt reconsideration of alternative inflammatory diagnoses. The coexistence of cerebral and chronic portal venous thrombosis raises the possibility of a systemic inflammatory or prothrombotic contribution, although a direct causal relationship with sarcoidosis could not be established. Clinical improvement following corticosteroid-based immunosuppression with methotrexate supports the working diagnosis, but the absence of tissue confirmation remains an important limitation.

title: Umbilical Cord Hernia is Not an Isolated Pathology: High Rate of Associated Anomalies in a Tertiary Center Cohort
abstract: Abstract Purpose This study aimed to evaluate the clinical profile of umbilical cord hernia (UCH), a defect often considered a minor variant of omphalocele, with a specific focus on the prevalence and spectrum of associated congenital anomalies. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 45 neonates with anterior abdominal wall defects treated between August 2019 and July 2024. Patients were categorized into three groups: omphalocele (n = 15), gastroschisis (n = 19), and UCH (n = 11). Demographic data, prenatal diagnosis, associated anomalies, surgical management, and outcomes were analyzed. Results In the UCH group, six patients (54.5%) had at least one major associated anomaly. Major cardiac anomalies were present in 45.5% (5/11), chromosomal anomalies in 27.3% (3/11), and genitourinary anomalies in 36.4% (4/11) of patients. The spectrum included Tetralogy of Fallot, Trisomy 13, 18, 21, and genetic syndromes (e.g., 3MC syndrome). Four patients (36.4%) had isolated UCH. Mortality in the UCH group was 18.2%, exclusively occurring in patients with major associated anomalies. Conclusion Contrary to traditional belief, umbilical cord hernia is frequently associated with serious cardiac, chromosomal, and multisystemic anomalies. These findings necessitate a paradigm shift in management, advocating for comprehensive screening including echocardiography, renal ultrasound, and genetic evaluation in all neonates with UCH, similar to the standard for omphalocele.

title: Implementation of novel approaches for management and treatment of brain tumours
abstract: Primary brain tumours remain among the most difficult cancers to treat because of their molecular heterogeneity, infiltrative growth and the blood–brain barrier (BBB), which restricts drug delivery. For almost two decades, management of glioblastoma, the most common malignant primary brain tumour in adults, has rested on maximal safe resection followed by radiotherapy with temozolomide. Recent years have brought a more differentiated picture. Integrated molecular classification (WHO CNS5) and DNA methylation profiling have sharpened diagnosis; fluorescence-guided surgery and tumour treating fields have extended the established armamentarium; the IDH inhibitor vorasidenib (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.39; 95% CI 0.27–0.56 versus placebo) and BRAF/MEK inhibition with dabrafenib plus trametinib have delivered the first clearly biomarker-directed successes in adult and paediatric glioma respectively; and immunotherapy, including checkpoint blockade, dendritic cell vaccination and intraventricular CAR T cells, is under active investigation with mixed results. Regulatory approvals of vorasidenib (2024) and dordaviprone (2025) have since extended the biomarker-directed options, and ultrasound-mediated BBB opening illustrates a delivery-focused strategy. In parallel, machine-learning tools now support tumour classification, segmentation and response assessment, and are well placed to inform patient selection, end-point definition and trial design. This review summarises the clinical evidence for each approach, highlights pharmacological issues (CNS penetration, response end-points, safety and exposure–response relationships) and discusses barriers to implementation, including trial design, external validation of AI tools and equitable access.

title: Impact of Triple Assessment on Surgical Decision-making in Thyroid Nodule Management.
abstract: Accurate preoperative assessment of thyroid nodules is crucial for distinguishing malignant from benign lesions and making optimal decisions. Triple assessment using clinical examination, ultrasonography (USG), and fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) has been increasingly used to improve diagnostic accuracy. The aim of the study was to evaluate the efficacy of triple assessment in the detection and treatment of thyroid nodules by correlating ultrasonographic findings, clinical evaluation, and FNAC results with histopathological diagnosis. This study was a prospective observational study of 56 patients with thyroid nodules undergoing surgical management. Data were collected prospectively using structured case record forms. Baseline information, physical examination findings, USG features, FNAC records, operative details, and histopathological reports were documented. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Frequency and percentage were used to present categorical variables. The diagnostic accuracy of clinical examination, USG, FNAC, and triple assessment was evaluated by estimating specificity, sensitivity, negative predictive value (NPV), positive predictive value, and diagnostic accuracy. A higher proportion of participants were female (85.7%) and were in the 41-60 years old age group. Histopathology confirmed benign lesions in 57.14% and malignant lesions in 42.86% of cases. Triple assessment achieved the most effective diagnostic accuracy, showing a sensitivity of 100%, a specificity of 87.50%, with a NPV of 100% and an overall diagnostic accuracy of 97.86%. Triple assessment is a dependable and useful modality for assessing thyroid nodules. Combined use of clinical examination, USG, and FNAC reduces false-negative results and supports appropriate clinical decision-making.

title: Evaluating the Interplay and Impact of Quality and Technical Variations on Performance of AI Models in Multi-Institutional Prostate MRI Datasets
abstract: Purpose: To evaluate whether visually assessed high-quality prostate MRI, as defined by the Prostate Imaging Quality (PI-QUAL) scoring system, is sufficient to ensure consistent AI model performance, or whether hidden acquisition-related technical effects introduce variability that cannot be detected through visual inspection. Methods: This retrospective study included 568 bpMRI scans from seven institutions, classified using PI-QUAL v2 into high-quality (scores 2-3) and low-quality (score 1) groups. Quantitative image quality features were extracted using MRQy from T2w and ADC sequences. Three experiments were conducted on high-quality scans: (1) unsupervised clustering to identify hidden technical batch effects; (2) V-Net models (M) for prostate capsule segmentation on T2w using single-cluster and balanced multi-cluster training strategies; and (3) VoxelMorph-based deformable registration (M2) to align ADC maps to T2w images. Performance metrics included DSC, precision, recall, volume ratio, HD95, ASSD, and TRE. Kruskal-Wallis tests assessed cross-cluster variability, Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) evaluated performance equivalence, and bootstrap resampling quantified training efficiency. Results: Clustering identified four clusters among 277 high-quality bpMRI scans. Single-cluster models showed variable performance (DSC=0.41-0.85) with significant batch effects (p<0.001), even with 140 training samples. The balanced multi-cluster model (n=60) eliminated batch effects (p=0.075), achieved equivalent performance (p<0.001), and demonstrated 2.23-fold greater training efficiency despite using 2.3-fold fewer samples. Registration performance also varied significantly across clusters (TRE=0.86-5.47 mm, p<0.001). Conclusion: Acquisition-related batch effects significantly impact AI generalizability in prostate MRI, even among high-quality scans. Quantitative clustering enables detection of technical variations and supports diversity-aware training strategies that achieve equivalent performance with 2.3-fold fewer samples while eliminating batch effects.

title: Longitudinal changes in motor network activity and connectivity in patients with suspected Transcient Ischemic Attack: an exploratory fMRI study
abstract: Background: and Objectives Transient ischemic attack (TIA) diagnosis is challenging because it relies mainly on clinical assessment and exclusion of common differential. Functional MRI (fMRI) may provide a diagnostic biomarker by detecting transient brain dysfunction not visible on conventional imaging. This pilot study aimed to characterize acute motor-task BOLD activation in patients with suspected DWI-negative TIA and compare functional patterns between confirmed TIA and alternative diagnoses. Secondary objectives were to assess longitudinal changes in activation and connectivity at 3 months. Methods In this prospective single-center study, adults presenting within 24 h of transient anterior-circulation neurological symptoms underwent conventional MRI and additional motor-task fMRI. Patients with acute DWI lesions were excluded. Final diagnosis was established after 3-month follow-up. Whole-brain analyses, individualized motor cortex region-of-interest (ROI) analyses, and generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) connectivity analyses were performed during the acute phase and at 3 months. Results Eight patients were enrolled; six had complete longitudinal imaging data and were included in the final analyses. Final diagnoses were TIA (n=2), migraine aura (n=2), functional neurological disorder (n=1), and hypoglycemia (n=1). Whole-brain and ROI analyses showed reduced bilateral motor-related BOLD responses during the acute phase in both TIA patients and in the patient with hypoglycemia. In contrast, patients with migraine and functional neurological disorder exhibited less marked longitudinal changes. In TIA patients, motor cortex activation increased at 3 months, tending to normalize toward values observed in non-TIA participants. Connectivity analyses revealed heterogeneous patterns, but the 2 TIA patients demonstrated increased longitudinal connectivity between the motor cortex contralateral to symptoms and other sensorimotor regions, including supplementary motor, premotor, parietal, and postcentral cortices. Discussion These preliminary findings suggest that TIA may be associated with transient bilateral reductions in motor-network activity. Functional abnormalities appeared to improve over time, supporting the hypothesis of reversible network dysfunction. Although limited by the very small sample size, this study provides the first longitudinal assessment of emergency task-based fMRI in rigorously defined TIA and supports further investigation of acute functional MRI as a potential biomarker of transient cerebral dysfunction.

title: Longitudinal associations between neuropsychiatric symptoms, structural and perfusion MRI changes in older adults with Mild Cognitive Impairment
abstract: Neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) are highly prevalent in Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), conceptualized as an intermediate clinical state between normal aging and dementia. Although neuroimaging studies have reported associations between NPS and brain alterations in MCI, longitudinal evidence on NPS and their relationship with multimodal MRI measures remains limited. We aimed to investigate (1) longitudinal changes in NPS, volumetric assessment and measurement of regional cerebral blood flow (CBF) within the medial temporal lobe (MTL); (2) associations between longitudinal changes in MRI measures and NPS; (3) whether baseline MRI measures predicted longitudinal changes in NPS. Thirty individuals with MCI aged over 65 years were recruited, of whom eighteen followed up for a mean period of 29 ± 8.9 months. There were significant reductions in total grey matter and white matter volumes, together with volume loss in the bilateral hippocampus, bilateral parahippocampal gyrus and right entorhinal cortex (pFDR≤0.05) over the follow up period. Volume loss in the right parahippocampal gyrus was associated with increase in aggression (pFDR<0.01), and CBF increase in the right hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus was associated with worsening in agitation (pFDR<0.01). Furthermore, lower baseline volume of the right entorhinal cortex was associated with increase in aggression, and lower baseline CBF in the right hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus was associated with worsening of agitation (pFDR<0.05). Our findings highlight the importance of identifying NPS in individuals with MCI and the role of structural and perfusion MRI measures as promising biomarkers for monitoring disease progression and improving risk prediction of conversion to dementia.

title: Vascular Proximity Coverage: A Novel CT-Based Marker of Pulmonary Vascular Distance to the Lung Parenchyma
abstract: Rationale: Conventional CT-derived pulmonary vascular metrics quantify vascular pruning but do not assess the spatial heterogeneity of vascular architecture. In COPD, peripheral microvascular pruning coexists with compensatory central vessel dilation, paradoxically preserving total vessel volume while reducing effective vascular penetration into lung parenchyma. Objectives: To develop and evaluate Vascular Proximity Coverage (VPC), a distance-based CT biomarker quantifying the spatial efficiency of pulmonary vascular distribution. Methods: This retrospective analysis included 7,881 COPDGene participants [PHASE] with complete vascular segmentations. VPC was estimated by integrating the area under the cumulative lung tissue coverage curve at distances of 0-10 mm from segmented vessel voxels. Multivariable models assessed associations with lung function, six-minute walk distance (6MWD), St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) score, mMRC dyspnea score, and all-cause mortality over a median follow-up of [10.8] years, adjusting for demographics, smoking, emphysema, scanner type, and BV5. The cohort was stratified at median BV5 and VPC into concordant (high/high, low/low) and discordant (high-BV5/low-VPC, low-BV5/high-VPC) vascular phenotypes. Results: VPC declined across disease severity (5.82 {+/-} 0.50 [UNITS] in non-smokers to 5.21 {+/-} 0.64 in GOLD 4; p < 0.001). Among spirometrically normal smokers, current smokers had lower VPC than former smokers (5.31 vs. 5.68; p < 0.001). Each standard deviation decrease in VPC was independently associated with reduced 6MWD ({beta} = -16.8 m, 95% CI: -19.5 to -14.0), worse SGRQ ({beta} = 1.9, 95% CI: 1.4 to 2.4), and greater dyspnea (RR = 1.05, 95% CI: 1.03 to 1.08; all p < 0.001). The lowest VPC quartile was associated with 38% higher mortality than the reference quartile (HR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.18 to 1.62; p < 0.001). The high-BV5/low-VPC phenotype showed 24% higher mortality than high-BV5/high-VPC (HR = 1.24, 95% CI: 1.08 to 1.42; p = 0.002) despite preserved vessel volume. Conclusions: VPC captures spatial heterogeneity of vascular architecture independent of vessel volume, is reduced in smokers without airflow obstruction, and identifies excess mortality risk among individuals whose total vessel volume appears preserved.

title: Deep Learning-Based Anatomical Level Classification of Craniofacial CT Slices: Comparison of CNN Architectures and Ensemble Methods
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) interpretation requires recognition of the anatomical level of each slice. Classification may facilitate preprocessing and AI-assisted fracture diagnosis. We developed deep learning models to classify craniofacial CT slices into six anatomical categories. A total of 11,769 images were collected from a multicenter database involving 10 Japanese university hospitals and the public Head-Neck-Radiomics-HN1 dataset. Patients were divided into training (70%) and evaluation (30%) sets. Five CNN architectures were trained from scratch, and hard- and soft-voting ensembles were evaluated. Individual-model accuracy ranged from 94.72% to 96.09%; the hard-voting ensemble achieved 96.46% accuracy (Cohen's k = 0.954). Although performance differed among individual models (Cochran's Q = 99.29, p < 0.001), the ensemble did not significantly outperform EfficientNetV2B1 (McNemar's p = 0.163). Errors occurred mainly between adjacent anatomical regions. Deep learning can classify craniofacial CT slices accurately and may support automated dataset organization and AI-assisted fracture diagnosis. External validation is needed.
